q: What is the final product of the sequence shown?
h: Track the carbon count: which steps add a carbon, and which only change the functional group?
w: Step 1 makes the aryl Grignard; CO2 then H3O+ give 4-methoxybenzoic acid (one new carbon). LiAlH4 reduces the acid to the primary benzylic alcohol, PBr3 converts it to ArCH2Br, and cyanide displaces bromide by SN2, adding a second new carbon: 2-(4-methoxyphenyl)acetonitrile. Net result: Ar–Br became Ar–CH2–C≡N, two carbons added.
x: This counts only one new carbon. The CO<sub>2</sub> carbon becomes the CH<sub>2</sub> after reduction and bromination, and cyanide brings a second carbon, so the nitrile sits on a CH<sub>2</sub>, not on the ring.
Nothing in the sequence hydrolyzes the nitrile; NaCN in DMSO stops at R–C≡N. Hydrolysis to the acid would need hot H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> or NaOH as a further step.
This adds three carbons. Only CO<sub>2</sub> and CN<sup>−</sup> add carbon here, so the chain off the ring has two carbons, not three.

q: What is the major final product of the sequence shown?
h: Dehydration of the tertiary alcohol can give an alkene inside the ring or outside it. Which is more stable, and what does ozone do to a ring C=C?
w: The Grignard adds to the ketone to give 1-ethylcyclohexan-1-ol. Hot H2SO4 dehydrates it by E1; the major alkene is the endocyclic 1-ethylcyclohexene (trisubstituted, in the ring, the more stable choice for a six-membered ring). Ozonolysis with a reductive (CH3)2S workup cuts the ring C=C, so the ring opens into one chain: the substituted carbon becomes a ketone and the CH becomes an aldehyde. Product: 6-oxooctanal, CH3CH2CO(CH2)4CHO.
x: Cyclohexanone plus acetaldehyde would come from the exocyclic alkene, ethylidenecyclohexane. Dehydration favors the endocyclic C=C, and cutting a ring alkene opens the ring instead of releasing the original ketone.
Dimethyl sulfide is a reductive workup, so the aldehyde end survives as CHO. A carboxylic acid would need an oxidative workup such as H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>.
This is the product after step 2 only. Hot H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> dehydrates a tertiary alcohol readily, and O<sub>3</sub> then cleaves the alkene.

q: Which sequence gives 1-(3-chlorophenyl)propan-1-one (shown) from benzene as the major product?
c: 1. CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COCl, AlCl<sub>3</sub>  2. Cl<sub>2</sub>, FeCl<sub>3</sub>  3. Zn(Hg), HCl
h: The two groups are meta to each other. Which of the two is a meta director, and so must go on first?
w: The acyl group (a ketone) withdraws electrons by resonance and is a meta director; chlorine is an ortho/para director. To get the 1,3 pattern, put the acyl group on first by Friedel–Crafts acylation (no rearrangement, no polyacylation), then chlorinate: Cl enters meta to the ketone. 1. CH3CH2COCl, AlCl3 2. Cl2, FeCl3.
x: Chlorine on first directs the acyl group ortho/para, mostly para, giving 1-(4-chlorophenyl)propan-1-one.
A primary propyl cation rearranges to the isopropyl cation, so this makes cumene, and an alkyl group would then direct Cl ortho/para. It also never makes a C=O.
The first two steps make the target, but the Clemmensen reduction removes the C=O and gives 1-chloro-3-propylbenzene.

q: Which sequence converts cyclohexanol into N-methylcyclohexanamine (shown) as the major product?
c: 1. TsCl, pyridine  2. NaN<sub>3</sub>, DMSO  3. LiAlH<sub>4</sub>  4. H<sub>2</sub>O
h: The target is a secondary amine with exactly one methyl on N. Which route forms the C–N bond and stops cleanly at that stage?
w: PCC oxidizes the secondary alcohol to cyclohexanone. With methylamine at pH ≈ 6 the ketone forms an iminium ion, which NaBH3CN reduces much faster than it reduces the ketone. This reductive amination gives the secondary amine without over-alkylation: 1. PCC, CH2Cl2 2. CH3NH2, NaBH3CN, pH ≈ 6.
x: This forms the imine, N-cyclohexylidenemethylamine (C=N), but nothing reduces it, so no amine is obtained.
This route gives cyclohexanamine, a primary amine with no N-methyl group (and the 2° tosylate also loses some material to E2).
Excess CH3I does not stop at one methyl: the amine is methylated all the way to the quaternary ammonium salt, N,N,N-trimethylcyclohexanaminium iodide.

q: Which sequence converts methyl 4-acetylbenzoate into 1-[4-(hydroxymethyl)phenyl]ethan-1-one, as shown?
h: The ester must be reduced while the more reactive ketone is left alone. How can the ketone be hidden from the reducing agent?
w: Only LiAlH4 reduces the ester to a primary alcohol, but it would also reduce the ketone. Protect the ketone first as a cyclic acetal (ethylene glycol, TsOH); acetals do not react with hydride. LiAlH4 then reduces the ester to CH2OH, and aqueous acid removes the acetal to restore the ketone: 1. HOCH2CH2OH, TsOH 2. LiAlH4 3. H3O+.
x: NaBH<sub>4</sub> reduces the ketone, not the ester, giving methyl 4-(1-hydroxyethyl)benzoate: the opposite of what is needed.
Without protection LiAlH<sub>4</sub> reduces both carbonyls, giving the diol 1-[4-(hydroxymethyl)phenyl]ethan-1-ol.
The protection step is right, but NaBH<sub>4</sub> is too weak to reduce an ester, so after deprotection the starting material comes back.

q: What is the final product of the sequence shown?
h: Each NaNH<sub>2</sub>/R–Br pair adds one alkyl group to the alkyne. What stereochemistry does a poisoned catalyst give?
w: The two acetylide alkylations build oct-3-yne, CH3CH2C≡C(CH2)3CH3. H2 with Lindlar's (poisoned) catalyst adds one equivalent of H2 syn across the triple bond and stops at the alkene, giving (Z)-oct-3-ene.
x: The E alkene comes from a dissolving-metal reduction (Na or Li in NH3). Lindlar hydrogenation adds both H atoms to the same face.
Full reduction to the alkane needs an active catalyst such as Pt or Pd/C. Lindlar's catalyst is poisoned so it stops at the alkene.
Step 5 reduces the triple bond. Lindlar's catalyst does react with alkynes; it is alkenes it leaves alone.

q: Which sequence converts acetylene into hexanal?
h: Count carbons first, then decide which hydration of a terminal alkyne puts the oxygen on the end carbon.
w: Acetylene (2 C) + 1-bromobutane (4 C) gives hex-1-yne. Hydroboration with a bulky borane, (sia)2BH, puts boron on the terminal carbon (anti-Markovnikov); oxidation gives an enol that tautomerizes to the aldehyde: 1. NaNH2 2. CH3(CH2)3Br 3. (sia)2BH 4. H2O2, NaOH gives hexanal.
x: Hg<sup>2+</sup>-catalyzed hydration is Markovnikov: the oxygen goes to the internal carbon, giving the methyl ketone hexan-2-one.
1-Bromopentane gives hept-1-yne, so the anti-Markovnikov hydration makes heptanal, one carbon too many.
Ozonolysis cleaves the triple bond into pentanoic acid and CO<sub>2</sub>; it does not hydrate the alkyne.

q: Ethyl acetoacetate is treated with 1. NaOEt, 2. an alkyl halide R–X, and 3. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>, heat. Which R–X gives 5-methylhexan-2-one (shown) as the product?
h: The acetoacetic ester synthesis turns R–X into CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>2</sub>–R. Cut the target at the bond between the CH<sub>2</sub> next to C=O and the rest.
w: Alkylation of the acetoacetate enolate, then ester hydrolysis and decarboxylation of the β-keto acid, gives CH3COCH2–R. In 5-methylhexan-2-one, CH3COCH2– is attached to –CH2CH(CH3)2, so R = isobutyl and the halide is 1-bromo-2-methylpropane. It is primary (though β-branched), so SN2 alkylation works.
x: An isopropyl group gives CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>2</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>, 4-methylpentan-2-one, one carbon short. A secondary halide also alkylates poorly.
An isopentyl group gives CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>, 6-methylheptan-2-one, one carbon too many.
A tertiary halide cannot undergo S<sub>N</sub>2; the enolate acts as a base and gives 2-methylpropene by E2.

q: Which combination, followed by H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> workup, gives 1-phenylcyclopentan-1-ol (shown)?
h: Find the carbon bearing the OH. In a Grignard synthesis it was a carbonyl carbon, and the new C–C bond is one of its bonds.
w: The OH carbon is a ring carbon that also carries the phenyl group, so it was the C=O carbon of cyclopentanone, and the phenyl came from the Grignard reagent. Addition of PhMgBr to the ketone and acid workup give the tertiary alcohol: C6H5MgBr + cyclopentanone.
x: This gives cyclopentyl(phenyl)methanol, a secondary alcohol whose OH carbon lies outside the ring (it was the aldehyde carbon).
An alcohol has no C=O to attack. Its O–H proton simply destroys the Grignard reagent, giving benzene and a magnesium alkoxide.
Grignard reagents open epoxides at carbon, so this gives trans-2-phenylcyclopentan-1-ol, with OH and phenyl on adjacent carbons.

q: What is the final product of the sequence shown? (It forms as a racemate; stereochemistry is not shown.)
h: NBS chooses the weakest C–H bond. A bulky base on that bromide can only remove one kind of β-hydrogen. What does OsO<sub>4</sub> add?
w: NBS/hν brominates the benzylic carbon, because the benzylic radical is resonance-stabilized: 1-bromo-1-phenylpropane. Potassium tert-butoxide is a strong, bulky base, so E2 wins over SN2; the only β-hydrogens are on C2, giving the conjugated alkene 1-phenylpropene. OsO4/NMO adds two OH groups syn across the C=C: 1-phenylpropane-1,2-diol.
x: This diol needs a terminal alkene, which would require bromination at the end carbon. NBS brominates the benzylic position, not the CH<sub>3</sub>.
This would be substitution of the bromide by water, which is not one of the steps; also OsO<sub>4</sub> would then have no alkene to react with.
tert-Butoxide is too hindered to be a good SN2 nucleophile at a secondary carbon; it acts as a base and eliminates.

q: What is the final product of the sequence shown?
h: Draw the Diels–Alder ring first and number it from the carbon that bears the ester. Where is the new C=C, and what happens when ozone cuts it?
w: The Diels–Alder reaction gives methyl cyclohex-3-ene-1-carboxylate: the ester carbon is C1 and the new C=C is C3=C4. Ozonolysis with a reductive workup cuts C3=C4 into two CHO groups and opens the ring. C1 is then joined to C2–C3 (CH2CHO) on one side and C6–C5–C4 (CH2CH2CHO) on the other: methyl 2-(2-oxoethyl)-5-oxopentanoate.
x: Two equal CH<sub>2</sub>CHO arms would need the C=C to be equally far from C1 on both sides. In the cyclohexene ring C1 is two bonds from one alkene carbon and three from the other.
(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>S is a reductive workup, so the cleaved ends stay as aldehydes, not carboxylic acids.
This is only the Diels–Alder adduct. Ozone readily cleaves the isolated ring C=C in steps 2 and 3.

q: Which sequence converts 3-phenylpropanoic acid into 2-phenylethan-1-amine, with one fewer carbon, as shown?
c: 1. LiAlH<sub>4</sub>; H<sub>2</sub>O  2. PBr<sub>3</sub>  3. NaN<sub>3</sub>  4. LiAlH<sub>4</sub>; H<sub>2</sub>O
1. SOCl<sub>2</sub>  2. NH<sub>3</sub> (excess)  3. P<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub>, heat  4. LiAlH<sub>4</sub>; H<sub>2</sub>O
h: Only one amide reaction loses the carbonyl carbon as CO<sub>2</sub>.
w: SOCl2 makes the acid chloride and NH3 converts it to the primary amide, 3-phenylpropanamide. In the Hofmann rearrangement (Br2, NaOH, H2O) the N-bromoamide rearranges to an isocyanate, which is hydrolyzed with loss of CO2. The C=O carbon is lost, giving the amine with one fewer carbon: 1. SOCl2 2. NH3 3. Br2, NaOH, H2O.
x: LiAlH<sub>4</sub> reduces the amide C=O to CH<sub>2</sub> and keeps every carbon, giving 3-phenylpropan-1-amine.
This keeps all three chain carbons (acid → alcohol → bromide → azide → amine), giving 3-phenylpropan-1-amine.
Dehydration gives the nitrile and LiAlH<sub>4</sub> reduces it to RCH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>, again 3-phenylpropan-1-amine with no carbon lost.

q:
Which sequences convert 1-methylcyclohexene into 2-methylcyclohexan-1-one (shown)?
I. 1. BH3·THF 2. H2O2, NaOH 3. PCC, CH2Cl2
II. 1. H2O, H2SO4 2. PCC, CH2Cl2
III. 1. BH3·THF 2. H2O2, NaOH 3. Na2Cr2O7, H2SO4
h: The oxygen must end up on the less substituted alkene carbon, and the alcohol made must be one that can be oxidized.
w: Hydroboration–oxidation is anti-Markovnikov: OH goes on C2, giving (trans)-2-methylcyclohexan-1-ol, a secondary alcohol. Any oxidant for secondary alcohols then gives the ketone. I is true (PCC). III is true: chromic acid also oxidizes a 2° alcohol to a ketone, and there is no aldehyde to over-oxidize. II is false: acid-catalyzed hydration is Markovnikov and gives 1-methylcyclohexan-1-ol, a tertiary alcohol that PCC cannot oxidize. I and III only.
x: This rejects III, but chromic acid oxidizes secondary alcohols to ketones cleanly; over-oxidation is a concern only for primary alcohols.
This accepts II. Acid hydration puts OH on the tertiary carbon, and a 3° alcohol has no C–H on the carbinol carbon to oxidize.
II fails: Markovnikov hydration gives a tertiary alcohol, which PCC does not oxidize.

q: The enone shown is made in one step by a crossed aldol condensation (NaOH, aqueous ethanol, heat). Which two starting materials are used?
h: Break the C=C. The alkene carbon on the ring was a C=O carbon; the other alkene carbon was the α-carbon of an enolate. Which partner has no α-H?
w: Disconnecting the C=C of the α,β-unsaturated ketone gives a CH=O on the aryl carbon and a CH3 next to the ketone C=O. So the electrophile is 4-methoxybenzaldehyde, which has no α-H and cannot enolize, and the enolate comes from acetone, CH3COCH3. Using excess acetone keeps the reaction from adding a second aryl group. Answer: 4-methoxybenzaldehyde + acetone, giving (E)-4-(4-methoxyphenyl)but-3-en-2-one.
x: Acetaldehyde's enolate gives (E)-3-(4-methoxyphenyl)prop-2-enal, an aldehyde with one carbon fewer; the target is a methyl ketone.
Butan-2-one adds an extra carbon: reaction at its CH<sub>3</sub> gives an ethyl ketone, and reaction at its CH<sub>2</sub> gives a branched enone. Neither is the target.
Acetaldehyde condenses mostly with itself, and the aryl ketone is the poorer electrophile. A cross product would be ArC(CH<sub>3</sub>)=CHCHO, an aldehyde, not the target ketone.

q: Which sequence converts bromobenzene into 2-phenylethan-1-ol?
h: The target has two carbons between the ring and the OH. Which electrophile adds two carbons and puts the oxygen on the far carbon?
w: Phenylmagnesium bromide opens ethylene oxide by SN2 attack at a ring carbon; the alkoxide is two carbons away, and acid workup gives 2-phenylethan-1-ol. Epoxides are the standard two-carbon extension that leaves a primary alcohol.
x: Formaldehyde adds only one carbon, giving benzyl alcohol (phenylmethanol).
Acetaldehyde adds two carbons, but the OH ends up on the carbon attached to the ring: 1-phenylethan-1-ol.
Ethanol is an acid toward a Grignard reagent; it simply protonates it to benzene.

q: A student plans to make cyclohexylmethanol from cyclohexanone as shown. Which statement about the plan is correct?
c: Step 2 is wrong: acid hydration is Markovnikov; BH<sub>3</sub>·THF then H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, NaOH gives the primary alcohol.
Step 1 is wrong: a Wittig reagent adds to the C=O to give a tertiary alcohol, not an alkene.
Step 2 is wrong: acid hydration is anti-Markovnikov; Hg(OAc)<sub>2</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>O then NaBH<sub>4</sub> gives the primary alcohol.
The plan works as written, because the exocyclic CH<sub>2</sub> is the less hindered carbon and takes the OH.
h: After the Wittig step the alkene is methylenecyclohexane. In acid, which carbocation forms?
w: The Wittig reaction correctly makes methylenecyclohexane. Aqueous acid protonates the CH2 end to give the tertiary carbocation, so water ends up on the ring carbon: 1-methylcyclohexan-1-ol, not the target. Hydroboration–oxidation adds OH to the less substituted carbon (anti-Markovnikov, no carbocation), giving cyclohexylmethanol. Step 2 is wrong; use BH3·THF then H2O2, NaOH.
x: Phosphorus ylides convert ketones into alkenes (C=O → C=CH<sub>2</sub>); the oxaphosphetane collapses to the alkene and Ph<sub>3</sub>P=O.
Acid hydration is Markovnikov, and oxymercuration is also Markovnikov, so it too would give 1-methylcyclohexan-1-ol.
Orientation in acid is set by carbocation stability, not by steric hindrance; the tertiary cation forms, so OH goes on the ring carbon.

q: What is the final product of the sequence shown? (Stereoisomers are not distinguished.)
h: LDA makes an enolate. Where does the enolate carbon attack, and what does NaBH<sub>4</sub> then reduce?
w: LDA removes an α-H to give the lithium enolate, which is alkylated at carbon by allyl bromide (SN2), giving 2-allylcyclohexan-1-one. NaBH4 reduces the ketone to the secondary alcohol and leaves the isolated C=C alone: 2-allylcyclohexan-1-ol (cis/trans mixture).
x: This puts the allyl group and OH on the same carbon, as if an allyl Grignard had added to the C=O. The enolate reacts at the α-carbon, and NaBH<sub>4</sub> then supplies only H.
This is the product after step 2. NaBH<sub>4</sub> reduces ketones readily.
O-Alkylation is minor for lithium enolates with alkyl halides; C-alkylation dominates. Also NaBH<sub>4</sub> would not change an enol ether.

q: Which sequence converts acetophenone into 1-(3-aminophenyl)ethan-1-one, as shown?
c: 1. Zn(Hg), HCl  2. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>  3. Fe, HCl  4. NaOH
h: Nitration goes meta to the acetyl group. Which reducing agent attacks the nitro group but not the ketone?
w: The acetyl group is a meta director, so nitration gives 3-nitroacetophenone. Iron (or tin) in HCl reduces an aryl NO2 to NH3+ and does not touch the ketone; NaOH frees the amine: 1. HNO3, H2SO4 2. Fe, HCl 3. NaOH.
x: NaBH<sub>4</sub> reduces the ketone to a secondary alcohol and leaves the nitro group, the opposite of what is needed.
LiAlH<sub>4</sub> reduces the ketone, and with aryl nitro groups it gives azo compounds rather than a clean amine.
The Clemmensen reduction removes the C=O first, giving ethylbenzene; the ethyl group directs ortho/para, and the ketone is gone.

q: What is the final product of the sequence shown? (It forms as a racemate.)
h: Find the weakest C–H bond for NBS, then follow the new carbon from cyanide.
w: NBS/hν brominates the benzylic CH2 (benzylic radical, resonance-stabilized), giving (1-bromoethyl)benzene. Cyanide displaces bromide (SN2 at a secondary benzylic carbon in DMSO), adding one carbon, and hot aqueous acid hydrolyzes the nitrile to the carboxylic acid: 2-phenylpropanoic acid (racemic).
x: A straight chain would need bromination at the CH<sub>3</sub> end. NBS brominates the benzylic carbon, so CN and then COOH end up on the carbon next to the ring.
This is the product after step 2; hot H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> hydrolyzes the nitrile through the amide to the carboxylic acid.
This acid has one carbon fewer and no methyl branch. The ethyl group's CH<sub>3</sub> stays in the product as the branch.

q:
Which sequences give 1-bromo-4-tert-butylbenzene (shown) from benzene as the major product?
I. 1. (CH3)3CCl, AlCl3 2. Br2, FeBr3
II. 1. Br2, FeBr3 2. (CH3)3CCl, AlCl3
III. 1. (CH3)2CHCOCl, AlCl3 2. Br2, FeBr3 3. Zn(Hg), HCl
h: Bromine and alkyl groups are both ortho/para directors; a bulky group strongly favors para. An acyl group is a meta director, and a Clemmensen reduction cannot make a quaternary carbon.
w: I is true: tert-butylbenzene (activated, o/p) brominates almost only para, because the tert-butyl group blocks its ortho positions. II is true: bromobenzene is only weakly deactivated, so Friedel–Crafts alkylation still works; Br directs o/p and the bulky tert-butyl cation goes para. III is false on two counts: the acyl group directs Br meta, and Clemmensen reduction of the isobutyryl group gives an isobutyl group, CH2CH(CH3)2, not tert-butyl. I and II only.
x: This rejects II. Friedel–Crafts reactions fail on strongly deactivated rings (NO<sub>2</sub>, C=O, SO<sub>3</sub>H), but a halobenzene still reacts, and Br directs the new group para.
This rejects I and accepts III. III gives 1-bromo-3-isobutylbenzene (meta, wrong alkyl group), while I gives the target.
III fails: the acyl group sends Br meta, and reducing C=O to CH2 gives an isobutyl group, not tert-butyl.
